Setup Section:
Note, if you already went through the previous demos and have your prams samples in your environment, you do not need to do this,
but I am putting a simplified setup chunk for those that do not. 
```{r}
### 1. Setup ----
library(haven)
library(dplyr)
library(effsize)
library(haven)
library(rcompanion)

### 2. Load data ----
prams <- read_sas("phase8_arf_2016_2021.sas7bdat")

### 3. Construct IPV variable ----
ipvv <- c("PAB6HUS", "PAB_XHUS", "PAD6HUS", "PAD_XHUS")

prams_IPV <- prams %>%
  filter(complete.cases(across(all_of(ipvv)))) %>%        # remove missing IPV rows
  filter(!if_any(all_of(ipvv), ~ . %in% c("B","T"))) %>%  # remove blank/teen-mom codes
  mutate(IPV = if_else(
    PAB6HUS == 2 | PAB_XHUS == 2 | PAD6HUS == 2 | PAD_XHUS == 2,
    2, 1
  ))

### 4. Create 1:1 sample (1000 yes / 1000 no) ----
set.seed(456)
prams11_sample <- bind_rows(
  prams_IPV %>% filter(IPV == 2) %>% slice_sample(n = 1000),
  prams_IPV %>% filter(IPV == 1) %>% slice_sample(n = 1000)
)

### 5. Create 1:3 sample (1000 yes / 3000 no) ----
set.seed(123)
prams13_sample <- bind_rows(
  prams_IPV %>% filter(IPV == 2) %>% slice_sample(n = 1000),
  prams_IPV %>% filter(IPV == 1) %>% slice_sample(n = 3000)
)

### 6. Select final variables for modeling ----
vars_needed <- c(
  "YY4_DOB","HISPANIC","MAT_RACE_PU","MAT_AGE_PU","MARRIED","INSNONE","PP_NONE",
  "MAT_DEG","MAT_WIC","STRS_ARG","STRS_BIL","BPG_DEPRS8","MH_PGDX8","PGINTENT",
  "CIG_1TRI","CIG_2TRI","CIG_3TRI","CIG_PRIOR","OTH_TERM","MM_NOMD","TYP_INJR",
  "PRE_ABUS","PRE_MHDP","KOTELCHUCK","ASK_ABUS","ASK_DPRS","STATE","NEST_YR",
  "VITAMIN","IPV"
)

vars <- vars_needed[vars_needed %in% names(prams11_sample)]

prams11f <- prams11_sample[, vars]
prams13f <- prams13_sample[, vars]

```


Section 2: Chi squared tests: 
The chi‑square test checks whether two categorical variables are associated with each other.
It compares the observed counts in each category to the expected counts if there were no relationship.

Use it when both variables are categorical, usually with one binary (e.g., IPV vs Marital Status).
```{r}
#IPV vs. Marital status 
tbl_married <- table(prams13f$IPV, prams13f$MARRIED)
tbl_married

chisq.test(tbl_married)

#IPV vs. WIC status
tbl_wic <- table(prams13f$IPV, prams13f$MAT_WIC)
tbl_wic

chisq.test(tbl_wic)

#IPV vs. Depression
tbl_dep <- table(prams13f$IPV, prams13f$BPG_DEPRS8)
tbl_dep

chisq.test(tbl_dep)
```


Section 3: A t‑test compares the means of a continuous variable between two groups.
It answers the question: Is the average value different between IPV = 1 and IPV = 2?

Use it when the outcome is binary, the predictor is continuous, and data are roughly normally distributed (or sample size is large)
```{r}
#Maternal Age vs. IPV t-test
t.test(MAT_AGE_PU ~ IPV, data = prams13f)

#Smoking in the 1st trimester vs. IPV t-test 
t.test(CIG_1TRI ~ IPV, data = prams13f)
```


Section 4: Wilcoxon Ranked Test 
The Wilcoxon test compares the distributions of a continuous variable between two groups without assuming normality.
It uses ranks instead of raw values, making it more robust to skewed data.

Use it when the continuous variable is skewed or you want a non‑parametric alternative to the t‑test
```{r}
#Prior smoking history vs. IPV
wilcox.test(CIG_PRIOR ~ IPV, data = prams13f)

#OTH Term vs. IPV
wilcox.test(OTH_TERM ~ IPV, data = prams13f)
```


Section 5: Correlation between predictors
Same test as Section 1, but used to explore relationships between predictors, not between predictor and outcome.

This helps identify collinearity, overlapping constructs, variables that may not belong in the same model
```{r}
#WIC vs. Marital Status 
tbl_wic_married <- table(prams13f$MAT_WIC, prams13f$MARRIED)
tbl_wic_married

chisq.test(tbl_wic_married)

#Depression vs. Mental Health Diagnosis 
tbl_dep_mh <- table(prams13f$BPG_DEPRS8, prams13f$MH_PGDX8)
tbl_dep_mh

chisq.test(tbl_dep_mh)

```
